title: When and Why Do Linear Bias Probes Fail? A Geometric and Statistical Theory of Bias Detectability in Large Language Model Representations

paper.title: When and Why Do Linear Bias Probes Fail? A Geometric and Statistical Theory of Bias Detectability in Large Language Model Representations
paper.abstract: Abstract Linear probing is the standard instrument for detecting social biases in the hidden representations of large language models. Yet reported probe accuracies come almost exclusively from counterfactual evaluations in which every input carries an explicit demographic marker—a regime that turns out to be trivially easy (AUC ≈ 1.0 \approx 1.0 throughout our experiments). Once only a fraction α \alpha of inputs carries demographic information, performance degrades sharply, and a weak probe may reflect either an unbiased model or an underpowered detector. We develop a theory that resolves this ambiguity. Modeling representations as two class-conditional clusters with Mahalanobis separation s s on a manifold of curvature κ \kappa , we prove: (i) a finite-sample generalization bound governed by the manifold’s extrinsic radius—capped by positive curvature (Bonnet–Myers)—with a matching d B / n \smash{\sqrt{d_{B}/n}} minimax lower bound; (ii) an exact purity law for the maximum linear-probe AUC, strictly increasing in α \alpha ; (iii) a curvature ceiling : ambient chordal separation on a space form cannot exceed 2 / κ 2/\sqrt{\kappa} ; and (iv) a detectability threshold α ∗ ​ ( n ) ≈ 2.05 ​ ( z 1 − δ + z 1 − γ ) / ( s ​ n ) \alpha^{*}(n)\approx 2.05\,(z_{1-\delta}+z_{1-\gamma})/(s\sqrt{n}) below which no audit can distinguish probe output from chance. Every theorem is validated on synthetic manifolds with known ground truth and on six open-weight models × \times four bias dimensions, where the purity law predicts entire AUC– α \alpha curves from a single cross-fitted s ^ \hat{s} measured at α = 1 \alpha=1 , with no parameters fitted to those curves. Three further checks close the loop: the detection test is calibrated on exact nulls that replicate the full protocol; kernel and MLP baselines confirm that the curvature ceiling is specific to linear readout, whereas the purity law—a Bayes bound—caps nonlinear probes as well; and stereotype leakage in “neutral” text is measured against occupation statistics rather than assumed absent. The framework turns bias auditing into a power analysis: given a target purity and effect size, it prescribes the sample budget n ​ ( α ) n(\alpha) for a conclusive audit.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Consider an auditor tasked with certifying that a language model does not encode gender stereotypes. Following standard practice, she trains a logistic-regression probe on the model’s hidden states. On a benchmark of minimal counterfactual pairs (“ He is a doctor” vs. “ She is a doctor”), the probe separates the two classes perfectly: AUC = 1.0 =1.0 . On a realistic corpus, in which roughly seven of every ten sentences mention no demographic attribute at all, the same probe on the same model returns an AUC of 0.70 0.70 —and on a smaller audit sample of a hundred sentences with sparser markers, 0.55 0.55 , statistically indistinguishable from coin flipping. Which number should the audit report? Is the model saturated with gender information, moderately biased, or clean? Is the third probe telling us the bias is absent—or merely that the probe is blind? This paper develops the theory needed to answer such questions. Its central claim is that linear-probe performance is not an intrinsic property of a model: it is a joint function of the representation geometry (class separation s s , manifold curvature κ \kappa , intrinsic dimension d B d_{B} ), the signal purity α \alpha (the fraction of inputs that carry demographic evidence), and the sample size n n . All three appear in closed form in our results, and all three are measurable. Once they are measured, the probe’s behavior across regimes—including its apparent failures—becomes predictable, in several cases with no free parameters. The need for such a theory is practical. Linear probes underpin bias benchmarks, model cards, and debiasing pipelines: null-space projection and concept-erasure methods explicitly assume that bias occupies a linear subspace [ 61 , 62 , 13 ] , and intervention techniques steer behavior along probe directions [ 42 ] . Yet the field has repeatedly documented probe pathologies—probes that memorize dataset artifacts [ 37 ] , probes whose accuracy does not transfer to downstream harms [ 33 , 21 ] , and debiasing that hides rather than removes information [ 34 ] . What has been missing is a quantitative account of when a linear probe is a reliable instrument and when it is underpowered, and a way to tell an unbiased model from an underpowered audit.

sections.heading: I-A What the theory says
sections.text: We model the probing task generatively. A fraction α \alpha of texts carry a demographic marker and induce representations from one of two clusters whose centers are separated by Mahalanobis distance s s ; the remaining 1 − α 1-\alpha are neutral and carry no label information. The clusters live on (a neighborhood of) a submanifold whose sectional curvature is bounded by κ \kappa . Four results organize the paper. (1) Sample complexity (Theorem 1 , Proposition 1 ). The generalization gap of norm-bounded linear probes decays as n − 1 / 2 n^{-1/2} , with a complexity constant governed by the bias submanifold’s extrinsic radius—a quantity that a positive lower curvature bound provably caps, via the Bonnet–Myers diameter theorem—and with a matching minimax lower bound Ω ​ ( d B / n ) \Omega(\sqrt{d_{B}/n}) in the intrinsic dimension. The practical content is a budget rule: halving the audit’s uncertainty requires quadrupling n n . On space forms the cap tightens to the sphere radius, and there curvature helps generalization exactly where it hurts separability (Theorem 2 ). (2) Purity (Theorem 3 ). The best achievable AUC at purity α \alpha is exactly α 2 ​ Φ ​ ( s 2 ) + 2 ​ α ​ ( 1 − α ) ​ Φ ​ ( s 2 ​ 2 ) + ( 1 − α ) 2 2 \alpha^{2}\Phi(\frac{s}{\sqrt{2}})+2\alpha(1-\alpha)\Phi(\frac{s}{2\sqrt{2}})+\frac{(1-\alpha)^{2}}{2} . This function is strictly increasing in α \alpha and saturates at the binormal value Φ ​ ( s / 2 ) \Phi(s/\sqrt{2}) . Two consequences matter. First, the counterfactual regime ( α = 1 \alpha=1 ) with the large separations typical of surface demographic markers ( s ^ ≈ 8 \hat{s}\approx 8 – 40 40 in our measurements) sits deep in the saturated zone—AUC ≈ 1.0 \approx 1.0 conveys almost no information about s s beyond a loose lower bound, which is why counterfactual benchmarks overstate real-world separability. Second, monotonicity is a falsifiable prediction: no “inversion” or interior optimum of AUC as a function of purity is possible in this model class, and none is observed in our sweeps. (3) Curvature (Theorem 2 ). Linear probes operate on ambient coordinates, hence on chords of the representation manifold. On a manifold of curvature κ > 0 \kappa>0 , the chord subtended by geodesic distance r r has length 2 κ ​ sin ⁡ ( κ ​ r 2 ) ≤ min ⁡ ( r , 2 / κ ) \frac{2}{\sqrt{\kappa}}\sin(\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}\,r}{2})\leq\min(r,\,2/\sqrt{\kappa}) : ambient separation saturates at the manifold diameter scale 2 / κ 2/\sqrt{\kappa} no matter how far apart the classes are geodesically. (4) Detectability (Theorem 4 ). An audit is a hypothesis test. Because the null distribution of empirical AUC on a held-out sample is known exactly (a U U -statistic with variance n + + n − + 1 12 ​ n + ​ n − \frac{n_{+}+n_{-}+1}{12n_{+}n_{-}} ; Section V-E maps the working CV statistic onto this null and calibrates it empirically), there is a critical purity α ∗ ​ ( n ) ≈ 2.05 ​ ( z 1 − δ + z 1 − γ ) / ( s ​ n ) \alpha^{*}(n)\approx 2.05\,(z_{1-\delta}+z_{1-\gamma})/(s\sqrt{n}) below which no level- δ \delta test achieves power 1 − γ 1-\gamma . The ( α , n ) (\alpha,n) plane splits into a detectable and an undetectable phase with boundary slope − 1 2 -\tfrac{1}{2} on log–log axes. In the undetectable phase a null probe result is uninformative about the model —the honest report is “underpowered,” not “unbiased.”

sections.heading: I-B What the experiments show
sections.text: We validate on two levels. On synthetic manifolds where s s , κ \kappa , d B d_{B} , and α \alpha are known exactly, the closed forms hold to within 0.006 0.006 – 0.013 0.013 AUC (oracle scoring), estimators of s s , κ \kappa , and d B d_{B} are calibrated against ground truth, and the empirical detection boundary tracks α ∗ ​ ( n ) \alpha^{*}(n) . On six open-weight models across four bias dimensions, a single cross-fitted s ^ \hat{s} measured on counterfactual pairs predicts the entire AUC– α \alpha curve with no further tuning; the ( α , n ) (\alpha,n) detection phase diagram matches the predicted boundary; the generalization gap follows the n − 1 / 2 n^{-1/2} law; and layer-wise scans, leakage-controlled splits, and LLM-paraphrased naturalistic prompts probe the robustness of each conclusion. A third, adversarial tier targets the protocol itself: E9 measures the realized false-positive rate of the detection test on exact nulls that replicate the full pipeline, E10 adds kernel and MLP probes that separate the linear-specific curvature ceiling from the Bayes-limited purity law, and E11 measures—rather than assumes away—the stereotype leakage in nominally neutral text. All numbers in every table are generated by the released scripts directly from logged experiment outputs; each table caption names its source file.

sections.heading: I-C Contributions
sections.text: • A generative model of bias probing with three measurable control variables ( s s , κ \kappa – d B d_{B} geometry, α \alpha , n n ), under which we prove: a curvature-corrected generalization bound with matching minimax lower bound; an exact purity–AUC law; a curvature ceiling for ambient linear separation; and a sharp detectability threshold α ∗ ​ ( n ) \alpha^{*}(n) (Section IV ). • A validated measurement pipeline: cross-fitted Mahalanobis separation (removing the O ​ ( d / n ) O(d/n) plug-in inflation), a label-free concentration index β B ∈ [ 0 , 1 − 1 / d ] \beta_{B}\in[0,1-1/d] with a proven link to separation and curvature, and estimators validated on ground-truth manifolds before being applied to LLMs (Sections V – VI ). • A two-tier validation—synthetic with known truth, then six LLMs × \times four bias dimensions—in which the theory’s zero-free-parameter predictions are tested and their errors reported as measured (Section VI ). • A reframing of bias auditing as power analysis, with explicit sample budgets n ​ ( α ) n(\alpha) and an “underpowered vs. unbiased” decision rule for null results (Section VII ).

sections.heading: II-A Bias measurement in NLP representations
sections.text: Bolukbasi et al. [ 15 ] showed that gender associations in static word embeddings admit approximately linear structure, and Caliskan et al. [ 16 ] quantified human-like associations with WEAT. Sentence- and context-level successors include SEAT [ 48 ] , StereoSet [ 51 ] , CrowS-Pairs [ 53 ] , BBQ [ 57 ] , and coreference-based tests [ 74 , 64 ] . A parallel critical literature documents that these instruments disagree with one another and with downstream harms [ 33 , 21 , 14 ] , and that linear debiasing can mask rather than remove information [ 34 ] . Our contribution is orthogonal to benchmark design: we treat any marker-based bias test as a detection problem and characterize its statistical power. The counterfactual/realistic gap we quantify (AUC 1.0 1.0 vs. 0.55 0.55 – 0.75 0.75 ) gives one mechanism for the poor correlation between intrinsic metrics and deployment behavior: intrinsic tests are usually run at α = 1 \alpha=1 , deployment corpora live at small α \alpha .

sections.heading: II-B Probing methodology and its critiques
sections.text: Linear probes were introduced as diagnostic classifiers [ 2 , 19 ] and remain the default tool for representation analysis [ 65 , 44 , 38 , 11 ] . Methodological critiques motivated control tasks and selectivity [ 37 ] , information-theoretic probes [ 58 ] , minimum-description-length probes [ 71 ] , and behavioral tests of whether probed information is used [ 26 ] . Concept-removal methods—INLP [ 61 ] , R-LACE [ 62 ] , LEACE [ 13 ] —assume linear geometry, as do inference-time interventions [ 42 ] , representation-engineering pipelines that extract and steer concept directions at scale [ 75 ] , single-direction behavioural mediation [ 7 ] , and sparse-autoencoder feature dictionaries [ 20 ] ; our power analysis applies to any such linear detector. Surveys of LLM bias instruments [ 31 ] catalogue the tests whose statistical power we characterize. We add the missing power analysis: control tasks ask whether a probe’s positive finding is trustworthy; our detectability threshold determines when a probe’s null finding is meaningful. Our grouped, template-disjoint cross-validation follows the leakage concerns of [ 37 ] .

sections.heading: II-C Geometry of neural representations
sections.text: The linear-representation hypothesis holds that high-level concepts occupy linear directions [ 49 , 8 , 56 ] , with supporting evidence for truth [ 47 ] , sentiment [ 66 ] , space and time [ 35 ] , and board-game state [ 52 ] . Complementary work measures the nonlinear side: anisotropy [ 27 , 50 ] , intrinsic dimension [ 6 , 1 , 68 , 69 ] , and visualizable manifold structure [ 63 ] . Manifold assumptions in learning theory go back to [ 12 , 54 , 29 ] . We connect these threads to bias probing through comparison geometry: curvature bounds control both covering numbers (hence sample complexity, via Günther’s volume comparison [ 32 , 24 ] ) and the chord-versus-geodesic contraction that limits ambient linear separability.

sections.heading: II-D Information geometry and statistical foundations
sections.text: Information geometry equips statistical models with the Fisher metric [ 3 , 5 , 17 , 55 ] ; applications to deep learning include natural gradient [ 4 ] , Fisher spectra [ 39 ] , and capacity measures [ 43 ] . Our generalization analysis uses Rademacher complexity and chaining [ 10 , 25 , 72 , 70 ] ; the lower bound uses Assouad’s method [ 67 ] . The AUC analysis rests on the binormal ROC model [ 36 ] and Fisher’s linear discriminant [ 30 ] and on exact null properties of the Mann–Whitney statistic [ 46 , 9 , 22 ] . Covariance estimation in the d ≳ n d\gtrsim n regime uses shrinkage [ 40 , 18 ] ; intrinsic dimension estimation uses maximum likelihood [ 41 , 45 ] with the two-NN estimator [ 28 ] as a cross-check. Relative to this toolbox our novelty is the assembly: an exact, checkable pipeline from measurable geometry to probe power.

sections.heading: V Experimental Design
sections.text: The experiments are designed so that each theorem is tested where its assumptions are known to hold (synthetic manifolds, Part E3) before being applied where they are approximations (LLM representations, E1–E2, E4–E7). All code, prompts, seeds, and raw outputs are released; every table names its source JSON file. We highlight design choices that target reproducibility problems documented in the probing literature.

sections.heading: V-A Theory-to-experiment map
sections.text: Because each closed form consumes measured inputs, we state the full chain from theorem to number once, explicitly (Table II ). Two conventions apply throughout. First, a prediction is called zero-free-parameter when no parameter is fitted to the data being predicted; its inputs may still be estimates (e.g. s ^ \hat{s} ), and the estimation error of those inputs is part of the reported prediction error, not an excuse for it. Second, every theorem is exact only under its stated assumptions; on LLM features the theorems are used through estimator plug-ins, and the two calibration experiments (E3-D for the estimators, E9 for the test) bound how much that translation can distort the conclusions. sections.heading: V-B Models and bias dimensions
sections.text: Six open-weight models: the GPT-2 family at four scales—Small (124M), Medium (355M), Large (774M), XL (1.5B) [ 60 ] —BERT-base-uncased (110M) [ 23 ] , and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [ 59 ] . This spans a 60 × 60\times parameter range, both decoder and encoder architectures, and base versus instruction-tuned training. Four bias dimensions: gender , race , religion , age . These counts (six models, four dimensions) are the same everywhere in the paper.

sections.heading: V-C Prompt construction with leakage control
sections.text: Prompts are generated from a template grid: 340 340 context cells (frame × \times content: 44 44 professions × 5 \times 5 frames, 20 20 traits × 3 \times 3 , 20 20 activities × 3 \times 3 ) crossed with 8 8 counterfactual marker pairs per dimension (e.g., man/woman , White person/Black person , Christian/Muslim colleague , young/elderly employee ), yielding 340 340 minimal pairs ( 680 680 marked sentences) per dimension. Crucially, the neutral pool ( 680 680 sentences per dimension) instantiates the same context cells with demographically unmarked heads ( person , individual ), so marked and neutral texts share an identical context distribution and the only systematic difference is the marker itself. A dataset of size n n at purity α \alpha contains α ​ n \alpha n marked sentences (balanced pairs, labels = = group) and ( 1 − α ) ​ n (1-\alpha)n neutral sentences with random labels—the operational meaning of “neutral texts carry no label information.” Two leakage controls follow [ 37 ] : (i) cross-validation folds are grouped by context cell , so no template context appears in both train and test folds of the same split; (ii) counterfactual pair members always travel together. A robustness subset (E1b) replaces templates with paraphrases generated by a locally served instruction-tuned model (via ollama ; the exact model tag is recorded with the released data), lexically validated to preserve the marker; this tests sensitivity to template regularity.

sections.heading: V-D Probing protocol
sections.text: Features are token-mean-pooled hidden states at the mid-depth layer (layer ⌊ L / 2 ⌋ \lfloor L/2\rfloor ; E4 scans all layers). Probes are ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -regularized logistic regressions ( C = 1 C=1 ) on standardized features, evaluated by grouped 5-fold cross-validation × \times 5 seeds; we report mean ± \pm s.d. and the across-seed range. Detection is a one-sided z z -test of the pooled out-of-fold AUC against the calibrated null scale 1.4 ​ σ 0 1.4\,\sigma_{0} (with σ 0 \sigma_{0} from Theorem 4 ) at level .05 .05 ; Section V-E states precisely how this statistic maps onto the theorem, why calibration is needed, and what the test’s measured level is. No result in this paper is reported as positive unless this test passes.

sections.heading: V-E The detection test under the CV protocol; null calibration; multiplicity
sections.text: Theorem 4 is exact for a single held-out sample scored by a fixed rule: conditionally on the scores, exchangeability of the labels under H 0 H_{0} makes AUC ^ \widehat{\mathrm{AUC}} the Mann–Whitney permutation statistic, whose null mean and variance do not depend on the score values. The working protocol departs from this ideal in two ways, and we treat both explicitly rather than assume them away. (i) Cross-validation. The pooled out-of-fold score of sample i i is produced by a probe trained on the other folds, so it depends on the training labels of those folds; scores and the label vector are then no longer independent under H 0 H_{0} , and exactness of σ 0 \sigma_{0} is not automatic. Label-flip symmetry of the training algorithm still forces 𝔼 ​ AUC ^ = 1 2 \mathbb{E}\,\widehat{\mathrm{AUC}}=\tfrac{1}{2} under H 0 H_{0} , but the variance must be checked. We therefore calibrate the test empirically: E9 replicates the entire pipeline—grid-structured pools, purity mixing, grouped folds, seeds, C = 1 C{=}1 probes—on label-free noise features, where H 0 H_{0} holds exactly, and measures the realized false-positive rate and the realized null s.d. of the pooled statistic (Section VI-B ). (ii) Seeds, and the measured null. The five seeds re-split one and the same sample, so the five pooled OOF AUCs are strongly dependent; treating them as independent replicates ( σ 0 / 5 \sigma_{0}/\sqrt{5} , the v14 build) is badly anti-conservative: its measured H 0 H_{0} rejection rate is 0.22 0.22 – 0.37 0.37 at nominal .05 .05 (E9). Testing the seed average against the unreduced σ 0 \sigma_{0} is much closer but still anti-conservative, because CV itself inflates the null s.d. of the pooled statistic above the i.i.d. value: E9 measures inflation factors of 1.20 1.20 – 1.31 1.31 across pool-respecting cells (and 1.9 × 1.9\times in the deliberately broken cell that resamples past the pool at α = 1 \alpha=1 , n = 1000 n=1000 , where duplicated points create ties), giving realized levels of 0.067 0.067 – 0.100 0.100 . We therefore calibrate : all detection claims in this paper test the seed-averaged statistic against 1.4 ​ σ 0 1.4\,\sigma_{0} , a multiplier chosen to cover the largest measured inflation with margin; its realized level on every pool-respecting E9 cell is at or below the nominal .05 .05 (Section VI-B , Table VIII ). The released JSONs retain the statistics from which the raw z z against σ 0 \sigma_{0} follows deterministically (AUC and n n ), so any alternative calibration can be applied by the reader. Families and multiple comparisons. Confirmatory detection claims form two families: F1, the E1 regime grid (all model–dimension–regime cells), and F2, the E2 purity curves ( 24 24 combos × \times 9 9 purities). We report, for each family, how many nominal .05 .05 detections survive Bonferroni ( .05 / m .05/m ) and Benjamini–Hochberg (FDR .05 .05 ) correction (Section VI-B ); the paper’s conclusions use only detections that survive. Phase-diagram cells are not individual claims but estimates of a detection rate compared against the α ∗ ​ ( n ) \alpha^{*}(n) frontier, and E9’s per-cell level check applies to them through the single-seed test they use. Released p-values are computed with the numerically stable survival function (the earlier 1 − Φ ​ ( z ) 1-\Phi(z) underflowed to 0 for z ≳ 8 z\gtrsim 8 ; the release notes document the fix).

sections.heading: VI-A E3: the theory is exact where its assumptions hold
sections.text: Table VI and Fig. 3 summarize the ground-truth tests. With oracle scoring (true discriminant direction), the mixture law ( 8 ) matches empirical AUC over 35 35 ( s , α ) (s,\alpha) settings to a maximum absolute error below 0.006 0.006 , and learned probes never exceed the bound beyond Monte-Carlo noise—consistent with ( 8 ) being the exact maximum. On spheres of known curvature, the chordal formula ( 6 ) matches oracle AUC to within 0.013 0.013 across a ( κ , r ) (\kappa,r) grid, and the qualitative signature of Corollary 1 is visible: flat-manifold AUC keeps rising with geodesic separation while curved-manifold AUC saturates at the ceiling (Fig. 3 b). Estimator calibration (Part D): κ ^ \hat{\kappa} recovers curvature with median relative error 0.17 0.17 (max 0.28 0.28 ) and correct ordering across κ ∈ [ 0.25 , 4 ] \kappa\in[0.25,4] ; d ^ B \hat{d}_{B} has median relative error ≈ 0.15 \approx 0.15 on spheres, with the known MLE underestimation growing with d d (up to ≈ 40 % \approx 40\% at d = 25 d{=}25 on linear manifolds; the Two-NN cross-check [ 28 ] shows the same downward drift), and the cross-fitted s ^ \hat{s} removes the plug-in inflation that would otherwise dominate at d / n > 1 d/n>1 . These are the error bars to keep in mind when the same estimators are read on LLM features. Two propagation checks quantify what these estimator errors can do to the theory’s predictions. First, perturbing κ \kappa by the ± 30 % \pm 30\% worst-case bias of the sagitta estimator moves the chordal prediction ( 6 ) by at most 0.021 0.021 AUC (median 0.003 0.003 ) over the E3-B grid, and the ceiling ( 7 ) by at most 0.041 0.041 over κ ∈ [ 0.25 , 8 ] \kappa\in[0.25,8] at the same noise scale: the curvature mechanism is robust to the estimator’s known bias. Second, the detectability boundary α ∗ ​ ( n ) \alpha^{*}(n) contains no curvature term, so κ ^ \hat{\kappa} bias cannot move it; its only estimated input is s ^ \hat{s} , and since α ∗ ∝ 1 / s \alpha^{*}\propto 1/s exactly, the median cross-fitted calibration error of E3-D shifts α ∗ \alpha^{*} by under 1 % 1\% . One scope note: σ w \sigma_{w} in ( 6 )–( 7 ) is a model quantity, known on the synthetic manifolds; it is never estimated on LLM features, and no LLM-side conclusion consumes it—on real features curvature enters only as the bounded, qualitative correction just described. sections.heading: VI-C E1: two regimes, one geometry
sections.text: Figure 4: E1 at a glance: probe AUC per model and bias dimension in the counterfactual ( α = 1 \alpha{=}1 , circles) and mixed ( α = 0.3 \alpha{=}0.3 , squares) regimes, with across-seed range intervals; open markers would indicate non-detection (none occur). The counterfactual row sits indistinguishably at the ceiling for all 24 24 pairs; the mixed regime separates from it by 0.27 0.27 – 0.33 0.33 AUC. Table III and Fig. 4 are the paper’s main measurement. Three facts are stable across all six models and four dimensions. (i) The counterfactual regime is saturated. All 24 24 model–dimension pairs probe at AUC = 1.000 ± 0.000 =1.000\pm 0.000 (three-decimal rounding) at α = 1 \alpha=1 , with cross-fitted separations s ^ ≈ 8 \hat{s}\approx 8 – 40 40 . By ( 8 ), any s ≳ 4 s\gtrsim 4 produces this ceiling: counterfactual AUC certifies the presence of surface-marker information but cannot rank models or dimensions—GPT-2 XL at s ^ ≈ 40 \hat{s}\approx 40 and Qwen2.5-7B at s ^ ≈ 8 \hat{s}\approx 8 receive the identical score. (ii) The mixed regime is informative. At α = 0.3 \alpha=0.3 and n = 300 n=300 , AUC falls between 0.67 0.67 and 0.73 0.73 . Every pair is detected, but all remain far from the ceiling. The zero-free-parameter Theorem 3 prediction (column “Purity-law pred.”, ≈ 0.755 \approx 0.755 for all saturated- s s pairs) upper-bounds the empirical values with a residual gap of 0.03 0.03 – 0.08 0.08 explained by finite-sample probe estimation: the theory is a maximum over probes, which the learned probe attains only as n → ∞ n\to\infty . (iii) The geometry is low-dimensional and mostly offset-clean. Intrinsic dimensions are d ^ B ≈ 4 \hat{d}_{B}\approx 4 – 7 7 . Measured neutral offsets are small relative to the class separation ( b w < s ^ / 2 b_{w}<\hat{s}/2 in 22 22 of 24 24 pairs; median ratio b w / ( s ^ / 2 ) ≈ 0.26 b_{w}/(\hat{s}/2)\approx 0.26 ), so the midpoint model of Assumption 1 is a good approximation. The two exceptions are the GPT-2 Medium and Large religion pairs (ratios ≈ 1.1 \approx 1.1 ), whose neutral pool sits beyond the class midpoint along the discriminant. By Corollary 2 the purity law remains monotone under any offset, and the offset perturbs the two middle mixture terms in opposite directions, which partially cancels: indeed these two pairs show no elevated prediction error in E2. With the leakage-controlled protocol and calibrated nulls, gender at α = 0.3 \alpha=0.3 , n = 300 n=300 is detectably above chance in all six models, and no below-chance AUC appears anywhere outside the undetectable phase (where AUC ≈ 0.5 ± \approx 0.5\pm noise is expected).

sections.text: For each model–dimension pair, s ^ \hat{s} is measured once on the α = 1 \alpha=1 marked set; equation ( 8 ) then predicts the entire AUC– α \alpha curve. Fig. 5 shows the curves; Table V reports the mean absolute error of the zero-parameter prediction and of a one-parameter fitted- s s reference, for all 24 24 pairs. We highlight three points. First, the empirical curves are monotone in α \alpha within seed noise in all 24 24 combinations ( 20 20 are exactly nondecreasing; the other four dip by at most 0.010 0.010 AUC between α = 0.02 \alpha=0.02 and 0.05 0.05 , within one seed s.d.)—the theory’s central qualitative prediction, with no trace of an interior optimum. Second, the zero-parameter prediction achieves median MAE 0.015 0.015 (max 0.048 0.048 ); the one-parameter fit improves this to median 0.010 0.010 . Because s ^ ≫ 4 \hat{s}\gg 4 throughout, the predicted curves collapse onto the saturated form 1 2 + α ​ ( 2 − α ) 2 \tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{\alpha(2-\alpha)}{2} : at high surface separation, purity—not geometry—is the binding constraint, and the collapse is real in the data. Third, the prediction error concentrates in BERT-base ( 0.025 0.025 – 0.048 0.048 across its four dimensions): the encoder’s learned probes sit furthest below the theoretical maximum at this n n , consistent with the bound interpretation (the theory caps, and finite-sample training determines how closely the cap is approached). The two large-offset religion pairs show no elevated error. One protocol caveat: each curve point reuses a single dataset draw across the five CV seeds, so its error bar reflects re-splitting only; at the smallest purities ( α ≤ 0.05 \alpha\leq 0.05 , i.e. ≤ 8 \leq 8 marked pairs at n = 300 n=300 ) dataset-level fluctuation, which these bars do not capture, can place individual points slightly above the population bound. Under family-wise correction, 159 159 of the 162 162 survive Benjamini–Hochberg at FDR .05 .05 , and 109 109 survive the (deliberately punitive for 216 216 dependent tests) Bonferroni threshold; no qualitative claim of this section rests on an individual near-threshold point. sections.heading: VI-F E4: layers
sections.text: Fig. 7 maps probe AUC over every layer of GPT-2 Small and BERT-base in both regimes. In the saturated counterfactual regime, layer choice is nearly irrelevant (AUC ≈ 1 \approx 1 at every depth)—another face of ceiling saturation. In the mixed regime, structure emerges, but not the folklore structure: the last layer is never optimal (choosing the best layer instead gains 0.9 0.9 – 6.0 6.0 AUC points; more for BERT than GPT-2), yet the optimal depth is model- and dimension-specific and is frequently an early layer (layer 1 1 – 2 2 in five of eight combinations). This is coherent with the nature of the signal: marker-based bias evidence is lexically anchored, and surface-lexical information is strongest in early layers. The practical guideline is therefore: avoid the last layer, and scan layers per model —the scan costs one forward pass and a handful of probe fits. sections.heading: VI-H E6: the generalization envelope
sections.text: At α = 0.3 \alpha=0.3 the train–test AUC gap decays with n n (Table VII , Fig. 9 ), but the working-protocol probe ( C = 1 C=1 ) decays with log–log slope ≈ − 0.09 \approx-0.09 , far shallower than − 1 2 -\tfrac{1}{2} . This is not a violation of Theorem 1 ; it is a lesson in reading it. The bound holds for a fixed norm budget Λ \Lambda , whereas the fitted ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -regularized probe spends a larger effective norm at small n n (its train AUC pins at ≈ 1 \approx 1 throughout)—the premise, not the inequality, changes with n n . sections.heading: VI-I E7: how far does a label-free diagnostic go?
sections.text: Fig. 10 closes the loop from geometry to prediction, with one negative and two positive results. Negative: the raw concentration index β B \beta_{B} does not rank real-model probe difficulty within a purity level (per- α \alpha Spearman ρ s ∈ [ − 0.34 , + 0.36 ] \rho_{s}\in[-0.34,+0.36] , none reliably positive; pooled ρ s = 0.09 \rho_{s}=0.09 ). Real LLM spectra violate the isotropic-noise premise of Lemma 2 —dominant non-signal variance directions swamp the top-eigenvalue signal—so the label-free shortcut fails exactly where its model assumption fails, and we report that plainly. Positive (supervised): the cross-fitted separation s ^ \hat{s} strongly ranks mixed-regime difficulty. Within purity levels, ρ s = 0.85 \rho_{s}=0.85 at α = 0.3 \alpha=0.3 ( p ≈ 1.4 × 10 − 7 p\approx 1.4\times 10^{-7} , n = 24 n=24 ) and 0.76 0.76 at α = 0.5 \alpha=0.5 ( p ≈ 1.8 × 10 − 5 p\approx 1.8\times 10^{-5} ); the full pipeline s ^ → \hat{s}\to Theorem 3 tracks empirical AUC across all 72 72 (model, dimension, α \alpha ) combinations with ρ s = 0.97 \rho_{s}=0.97 and MAE 0.033 0.033 (panel c). sections.heading: VI-L E11: how neutral is “neutral”? Measured stereotype leakage
sections.text: The purity model treats neutral texts as label-independent. E11 measures how far that idealization is from the truth of the representations, and how far our protocol is insulated from the difference. (A) The protocol is clean by construction. Strong classifiers (linear, RBF-SVM, MLP) trained on neutral-only features against the protocol’s randomly assigned labels probe at chance: 0 calibrated detections in 72 72 tests (max | AUC − 1 2 | = 0.069 |\mathrm{AUC}-\tfrac{1}{2}|=0.069 ), confirming that the random labeling used everywhere in E1–E7 admits no leakage into the reported numbers. (B) But the text is not semantically neutral. Assigning each of the 160 160 neutral profession sentences its WinoBias occupation-stereotype label [ 74 ] ( 16 16 professions overlap our inventory; 9 9 male-, 7 7 female-dominated per BLS), the α = 1 \alpha{=}1 marked-trained gender probe—never shown a neutral sentence—scores them at AUC 0.688 0.688 – 0.873 0.873 across the six models (all p ≤ 2.4 × 10 − 5 p\leq 2.4\times 10^{-5} ), largest for Qwen2.5-7B ( 0.873 0.873 ) and BERT-base ( 0.818 0.818 ); training directly on the neutral sentences reaches AUC 1.000 1.000 (linear, grouped CV) in every model. Occupation stereotype is thus fully linearly encoded in “neutral” representations, and the demographic-marker direction partially aligns with it. (C) Leaky purity stress test. Rebuilding the E2 gender sweep with neutral labels drawn from the stereotype with probability π \pi (the protocol is π = 1 2 \pi=\tfrac{1}{2} ; natural corpora with stereotype-correlated ground truth sit at π > 1 2 \pi>\tfrac{1}{2} ): at π = 1 2 \pi=\tfrac{1}{2} the curves are monotone within seed noise (max dip 0.043 0.043 , ≈ 1.8 {\approx}1.8 seed s.d.); at π = 0.75 \pi=0.75 the small- α \alpha tail lifts to a leakage floor of 0.64 0.64 – 0.69 0.69 (instead of decaying to 1 2 \tfrac{1}{2} ) and the curve is genuinely non-monotone (max dip 0.081 0.081 , beyond seed noise)—as it must be, since the theorem’s label-independence premise is violated; at π = 1 \pi=1 neutrals are simply labeled data and the curve pins at AUC ≈ 1 \approx 1 for all α \alpha . The practical translation: on corpora whose latent labels correlate with stereotypes, α \alpha measured by marker counting understates the effective signal, a null probe result is even harder to interpret, and the floor of the AUC– α \alpha curve estimates the leakage strength; our marker-based protocol sidesteps this by randomization, at the cost of modeling only marker-borne signal.

sections.heading: VII-A Guidelines for practitioners
sections.text: (1) Treat audits as power analyses. Before probing, fix the purity α \alpha of the audit corpus (measurable by counting marked texts) and the minimal effect size s min s_{\min} of interest; then budget n te ≥ ( z 1 − δ + z 1 − γ ) 2 / ( 3 ​ [ AUC max ​ ( α ; s min ) − 1 2 ] 2 ) n_{\mathrm{te}}\geq(z_{1-\delta}+z_{1-\gamma})^{2}\big/\big(3\,[\mathrm{AUC}_{\max}(\alpha;s_{\min})-\tfrac{1}{2}]^{2}\big) via ( 10 ) with σ 0 ≈ 1 / 3 ​ n te \sigma_{0}\approx 1/\sqrt{3n_{\mathrm{te}}} , or read n ​ ( α ) n(\alpha) off the phase diagram. If the audit statistic is a pooled cross-validated AUC rather than a single held-out split, multiply σ 0 \sigma_{0} by the E9 calibration factor ( 1.4 1.4 under our protocol; budget × 1.96 \times 1.96 )—or simply use one held-out split, for which σ 0 \sigma_{0} is exact. A null result below the frontier should be reported as underpowered . (2) Do not rank models by counterfactual AUC. Above s ≈ 4 s\approx 4 the ceiling hides all differences; rank by s ^ \hat{s} (cross-fitted) or by mixed-regime AUC at matched ( α , n ) (\alpha,n) . (3) Control template leakage—and measure it. We compare grouped (context-disjoint) with random cross-validation on identical data (E8, GPT-2 Small and Large, all four dimensions): with our design, in which marked and neutral prompts share one context grid, random CV inflates AUC by at most 0.011 0.011 ( α = 0.3 \alpha=0.3 ; < 10 − 4 <10^{-4} at the α = 1 \alpha=1 ceiling). The inflation is small because the design crosses markers with contexts; with organic corpora no such guarantee exists, so grouped CV remains the conservative default and the grouped–random gap is itself a cheap leakage meter. (4) Never the last layer—and scan. Away from saturation the last layer is uniformly suboptimal (E4), but the best depth is model- and dimension-specific and often early; a per-model layer scan costs one forward pass and recovers up to 6 6 AUC points. (5) Prefer cross-fitted effect sizes. Naive Mahalanobis plug-ins inflate catastrophically at d ≳ n d\gtrsim n (E3-D); any pipeline reporting raw separations at d / n > 1 d/n>1 without cross-fitting or shrinkage is suspect. (6) Do not trust raw β B \beta_{B} on real features. The label-free index ranks difficulty only when routed through the purity model ( 13 ) (E7: pipeline ρ s = 0.88 \rho_{s}=0.88 vs. raw ρ s ≈ 0 \rho_{s}\approx 0 ); with even a small labeled counterfactual set, the cross-fitted s ^ \hat{s} is the reliable diagnostic ( ρ s = 0.85 \rho_{s}=0.85 / 0.76 0.76 within the mixed regime at α = 0.3 \alpha=0.3 / 0.5 0.5 ). (7) Do not reach for nonlinear probes to rescue a weak audit. Against purity dilution no classifier can beat ( 8 ) (Remark 1 ); under ambient noise the curvature ceiling binds nonlinear probes too (E10-S2); and at audit-scale n n the kernel and MLP baselines lose more to variance than they recover (median − 0.068 -0.068 / − 0.015 -0.015 AUC, E10-R). Their legitimate use is diagnostic: a nonlinear probe that beats the linear one signals that the linear probe sits below its purity-law prediction, as in the BERT-base cases of E10.

sections.heading: VII-B Limitations
sections.text: Model of neutrality. Theorem 3 treats neutral texts as label-independent with a shared covariance. E11 measures how idealized that is: occupation-stereotype structure is fully linearly decodable from our “neutral” sentences (AUC 1.0 1.0 direct; 0.69 0.69 – 0.87 0.87 zero-shot from the marker direction), our protocol is insulated from it only because neutral labels are randomized, and under stereotype-correlated labeling ( π > 1 2 \pi>\tfrac{1}{2} ) the purity curve acquires a leakage floor and loses monotonicity—so the purity law should be applied to natural corpora only together with a leakage measurement of the E11-B type. Corollary 2 handles mean offsets; a full treatment of graded purity ( α \alpha as a distribution, leakage as a second signal component) is future work. Curvature on LLM features. Theorem 2 is exact on space forms; on LLM features our sagitta estimator carries 20 20 – 30 % 30\% bias (E3-D), so we use curvature as a bounded correction and a qualitative mechanism, not as a precisely measured quantity. Template ecology. Even with paraphrase robustness checks, template-derived prompts undercover the diversity of deployment text; purity in the wild also varies by domain. Scope of “bias.” Linear detectability of demographic markers is evidence about representations, not about downstream harms; bridging to behavioral bias metrics [ 33 , 21 ] remains open. Each dimension is moreover operationalized as a single binary marker contrast (man/woman, White/Black, Christian/Muslim, young/elderly) in English; multi-group, intersectional, non-lexical, and cross-lingual operationalizations are untested.

sections.heading: VIII Conclusion
sections.text: Throughout this paper “probe failure” has meant one operational thing: under the leakage-controlled protocol of Section V , the level- .05 .05 pooled-OOF detection test returns a null, or the measured AUC falls short of the theory’s maximum by more than the calibrated error of the pipeline. In that sense linear bias probes do not fail mysteriously. They fail for three quantifiable reasons—not enough marked signal ( α \alpha below the detectability frontier), not enough samples ( n n below the d B / n \sqrt{d_{B}/n} budget), or geometry that linear readout cannot exploit (chordal contraction under curvature)—and they succeed trivially in the counterfactual regime because surface markers put s s deep into the saturated zone of the purity law. Two boundaries of this account are now measured rather than conjectured. Nonlinear probes rescue neither mechanism: the purity law caps them provably (Remark 1 , confirmed in E10-S1), and under ambient noise even a geodesic oracle recovers none of the curvature-induced loss, while kernel and MLP probes trail the linear probe on real features at audit-scale n n (E10)—so the linear theory’s scope is, in practice, the scope of probing tout court in our regimes. And the neutrality idealization is measurably false of the text (stereotype signal is linearly decodable from “neutral” sentences, E11) yet harmless to our protocol by randomization, with the leaky-purity stress test mapping how it distorts audits on natural corpora. Under the stated assumptions—and with the detection test’s realized level verified on exact nulls (E9)—the combined pipeline predicts real probe behavior across six models and four bias dimensions from measured geometry, in the central case with no parameters fitted to the predicted curves. The practical payoff is a change of frame: a bias audit is a statistical power problem, and it should be designed—and its null results reported—accordingly.

A Geometric and Statistical Theory of Bias Detectability in Large Language Model Representations Mo Hai, Haifeng Li Abstract Linear probing is the standard instrument for detecting social biases in the hidden representations of large language models. Yet reported probe accuracies come almost exclusively from counterfactual evaluations in which every input carries an explicit demographic marker—a regime that turns out to be trivially easy (AUC ≈ 1.0 \approx 1.0 throughout our experiments). Once only a fraction α \alpha of inputs carries demographic information, performance degrades sharply, and a weak probe may reflect either an unbiased model or an underpowered detector. We develop a theory that resolves this ambiguity. Modeling representations as two class-conditional clusters with Mahalanobis separation s s on a manifold of curvature κ \kappa , we prove: (i) a finite-sample generalization bound governed by the manifold’s extrinsic radius—capped by positive curvature (Bonnet–Myers)—with a matching d B / n \smash{\sqrt{d_{B}/n}} minimax lower bound; (ii) an exact purity law for the maximum linear-probe AUC, strictly increasing in α \alpha ; (iii) a curvature ceiling : ambient chordal separation on a space form cannot exceed 2 / κ 2/\sqrt{\kappa} ; and (iv) a detectability threshold α ∗ ​ ( n ) ≈ 2.05 ​ ( z 1 − δ + z 1 − γ ) / ( s ​ n ) \alpha^{*}(n)\approx 2.05\,(z_{1-\delta}+z_{1-\gamma})/(s\sqrt{n}) below which no audit can distinguish probe output from chance. Every theorem is validated on synthetic manifolds with known ground truth and on six open-weight models × \times four bias dimensions, where the purity law predicts entire AUC– α \alpha curves from a single cross-fitted s ^ \hat{s} measured at α = 1 \alpha=1 , with no parameters fitted to those curves. Three further checks close the loop: the detection test is calibrated on exact nulls that replicate the full protocol; kernel and MLP baselines confirm that the curvature ceiling is specific to linear readout, whereas the purity law—a Bayes bound—caps nonlinear probes as well; and stereotype leakage in “neutral” text is measured against occupation statistics rather than assumed absent. The framework turns bias auditing into a power analysis: given a target purity and effect size, it prescribes the sample budget n ​ ( α ) n(\alpha) for a conclusive audit. I Introduction Consider an auditor tasked with certifying that a language model does not encode gender stereotypes. Following standard practice, she trains a logistic-regression probe on the model’s hidden states. On a benchmark of minimal counterfactual pairs (“ He is a doctor” vs. “ She is a doctor”), the probe separates the two classes perfectly: AUC = 1.0 =1.0 . On a realistic corpus, in which roughly seven of every ten sentences mention no demographic attribute at all, the same probe on the same model returns an AUC of 0.70 0.70 —and on a smaller audit sample of a hundred sentences with sparser markers, 0.55 0.55 , statistically indistinguishable from coin flipping. Which number should the audit report? Is the model saturated with gender information, moderately biased, or clean? Is the third probe telling us the bias is absent—or merely that the probe is blind? This paper develops the theory needed to answer such questions. Its central claim is that linear-probe performance is not an intrinsic property of a model: it is a joint function of the representation geometry (class separation s s , manifold curvature κ \kappa , intrinsic dimension d B d_{B} ), the signal purity α \alpha (the fraction of inputs that carry demographic evidence), and the sample size n n . All three appear in closed form in our results, and all three are measurable. Once they are measured, the probe’s behavior across regimes—including its apparent failures—becomes predictable, in several cases with no free parameters. The need for such a theory is practical. Linear probes underpin bias benchmarks, model cards, and debiasing pipelines: null-space projection and concept-erasure methods explicitly assume that bias occupies a linear subspace [ 61 , 62 , 13 ] , and intervention techniques steer behavior along probe directions [ 42 ] . Yet the field has repeatedly documented probe pathologies—probes that memorize dataset artifacts [ 37 ] , probes whose accuracy does not transfer to downstream harms [ 33 , 21 ] , and debiasing that hides rather than removes information [ 34 ] . What has been missing is a quantitative account of when a linear probe is a reliable instrument and when it is underpowered, and a way to tell an unbiased model from an underpowered audit. I-A What the theory says We model the probing task generatively. A fraction α \alpha of texts carry a demographic marker and induce representations from one of two clusters whose centers are separated by Mahalanobis distance s s ; the remaining 1 − α 1-\alpha are neutral and carry no label information. The clusters live on (a neighborhood of) a submanifold whose sectional curvature is bounded by κ \kappa . Four results organize the paper. (1) Sample complexity (Theorem 1 , Proposition 1 ). The generalization gap of norm-bounded linear probes decays as n − 1 / 2 n^{-1/2} , with a complexity constant governed by the bias submanifold’s extrinsic radius—a quantity that a positive lower curvature bound provably caps, via the Bonnet–Myers diameter theorem—and with a matching minimax lower bound Ω ​ ( d B / n ) \Omega(\sqrt{d_{B}/n}) in the intrinsic dimension. The practical content is a budget rule: halving the audit’s uncertainty requires quadrupling n n . On space forms the cap tightens to the sphere radius, and there curvature helps generalization exactly where it hurts separability (Theorem 2 ). (2) Purity (Theorem 3 ). The best achievable AUC at purity α \alpha is exactly α 2 ​ Φ ​ ( s 2 ) + 2 ​ α ​ ( 1 − α ) ​ Φ ​ ( s 2 ​ 2 ) + ( 1 − α ) 2 2 \alpha^{2}\Phi(\frac{s}{\sqrt{2}})+2\alpha(1-\alpha)\Phi(\frac{s}{2\sqrt{2}})+\frac{(1-\alpha)^{2}}{2} . This function is strictly increasing in α \alpha and saturates at the binormal value Φ ​ ( s / 2 ) \Phi(s/\sqrt{2}) . Two consequences matter. First, the counterfactual regime ( α = 1 \alpha=1 ) with the large separations typical of surface demographic markers ( s ^ ≈ 8 \hat{s}\approx 8 – 40 40 in our measurements) sits deep in the saturated zone—AUC ≈ 1.0 \approx 1.0 conveys almost no information about s s beyond a loose lower bound, which is why counterfactual benchmarks overstate real-world separability. Second, monotonicity is a falsifiable prediction: no “inversion” or interior optimum of AUC as a function of purity is possible in this model class, and none is observed in our sweeps. (3) Curvature (Theorem 2 ). Linear probes operate on ambient coordinates, hence on chords of the representation manifold. On a manifold of curvature κ > 0 \kappa>0 , the chord subtended by geodesic distance r r has length 2 κ ​ sin ⁡ ( κ ​ r 2 ) ≤ min ⁡ ( r , 2 / κ ) \frac{2}{\sqrt{\kappa}}\sin(\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}\,r}{2})\leq\min(r,\,2/\sqrt{\kappa}) : ambient separation saturates at the manifold diameter scale 2 / κ 2/\sqrt{\kappa} no matter how far apart the classes are geodesically. The resulting AUC ceiling Φ ​ ( 2 / ( κ ​ σ w ) ) \Phi\big(\sqrt{2}/(\sqrt{\kappa}\,\sigma_{w})\big) decreases monotonically from 1 1 (flat) to 1 / 2 1/2 ( κ → ∞ \kappa\to\infty ), giving the correct, legal-range replacement for curvature-based failure prediction, and quantifying what a geodesic-aware (nonlinear) probe could recover that a linear one cannot—a prediction E10 tests directly with kernel and MLP probes. (4) Detectability (Theorem 4 ). An audit is a hypothesis test. Because the null distribution of empirical AUC on a held-out sample is known exactly (a U U -statistic with variance n + + n − + 1 12 ​ n + ​ n − \frac{n_{+}+n_{-}+1}{12n_{+}n_{-}} ; Section V-E maps the working CV statistic onto this null and calibrates it empirically), there is a critical purity α ∗ ​ ( n ) ≈ 2.05 ​ ( z 1 − δ + z 1 − γ ) / ( s ​ n ) \alpha^{*}(n)\approx 2.05\,(z_{1-\delta}+z_{1-\gamma})/(s\sqrt{n}) below which no level- δ \delta test achieves power 1 − γ 1-\gamma . The ( α , n ) (\alpha,n) plane splits into a detectable and an undetectable phase with boundary slope − 1 2 -\tfrac{1}{2} on log–log axes. In the undetectable phase a null probe result is uninformative about the model —the honest report is “underpowered,” not “unbiased.” I-B What the experiments show We validate on two levels. On synthetic manifolds where s s , κ \kappa , d B d_{B} , and α \alpha are known exactly, the closed forms hold to within 0.006 0.006 – 0.013 0.013 AUC (oracle scoring), estimators of s s , κ \kappa , and d B d_{B} are calibrated against ground truth, and the empirical detection boundary tracks α ∗ ​ ( n ) \alpha^{*}(n) . On six open-weight models across four bias dimensions, a single cross-fitted s ^ \hat{s} measured on counterfactual pairs predicts the entire AUC– α \alpha curve with no further tuning; the ( α , n ) (\alpha,n) detection phase diagram matches the predicted boundary; the generalization gap follows the n − 1 / 2 n^{-1/2} law; and layer-wise scans, leakage-controlled splits, and LLM-paraphrased naturalistic prompts probe the robustness of each conclusion. II Related Work II-A Bias measurement in NLP representations Bolukbasi et al. [ 15 ] showed that gender associations in static word embeddings admit approximately linear structure, and Caliskan et al. [ 16 ] quantified human-like associations with WEAT. Sentence- and context-level successors include SEAT [ 48 ] , StereoSet [ 51 ] , CrowS-Pairs [ 53 ] , BBQ [ 57 ] , and coreference-based tests [ 74 , 64 ] . A parallel critical literature documents that these instruments disagree with one another and with downstream harms [ 33 , 21 , 14 ] , and that linear debiasing can mask rather than remove information [ 34 ] . Our contribution is orthogonal to benchmark design: we treat any marker-based bias test as a detection problem and characterize its statistical power. The counterfactual/realistic gap we quantify (AUC 1.0 1.0 vs. 0.55 0.55 – 0.75 0.75 ) gives one mechanism for the poor correlation between intrinsic metrics and deployment behavior: intrinsic tests are usually run at α = 1 \alpha=1 , deployment corpora live at small α \alpha . II-B Probing methodology and its critiques Linear probes were introduced as diagnostic classifiers [ 2 , 19 ] and remain the default tool for representation analysis [ 65 , 44 , 38 , 11 ] . Methodological critiques motivated control tasks and selectivity [ 37 ] , information-theoretic probes [ 58 ] , minimum-description-length probes [ 71 ] , and behavioral tests of whether probed information is used [ 26 ] . Concept-removal methods—INLP [ 61 ] , R-LACE [ 62 ] , LEACE [ 13 ] —assume linear geometry, as do inference-time interventions [ 42 ] , representation-engineering pipelines that extract and steer concept directions at scale [ 75 ] , single-direction behavioural mediation [ 7 ] , and sparse-autoencoder feature dictionaries [ 20 ] ; our power analysis applies to any such linear detector. Surveys of LLM bias instruments [ 31 ] catalogue the tests whose statistical power we characterize. We add the missing power analysis: control tasks ask whether a probe’s positive finding is trustworthy; our detectability threshold determines when a probe’s null finding is meaningful. Our grouped, template-disjoint cross-validation follows the leakage concerns of [ 37 ] . II-C Geometry of neural representations The linear-representation hypothesis holds that high-level concepts occupy linear directions [ 49 , 8 , 56 ] , with supporting evidence for truth [ 47 ] , sentiment [ 66 ] , space and time [ 35 ] , and board-game state [ 52 ] . Complementary work measures the nonlinear side: anisotropy [ 27 , 50 ] , intrinsic dimension [ 6 , 1 , 68 , 69 ] , and visualizable manifold structure [ 63 ] . Manifold assumptions in learning theory go back to [ 12 , 54 , 29 ] . We connect these threads to bias probing through comparison geometry: curvature bounds control both covering numbers (hence sample complexity, via Günther’s volume comparison [ 32 , 24 ] ) and the chord-versus-geodesic contraction that limits ambient linear separability. II-D Information geometry and statistical foundations Information geometry equips statistical models with the Fisher metric [ 3 , 5 , 17 , 55 ] ; applications to deep learning include natural gradient [ 4 ] , Fisher spectra [ 39 ] , and capacity measures [ 43 ] . Our generalization analysis uses Rademacher complexity and chaining [ 10 , 25 , 72 , 70 ] ; the lower bound uses Assouad’s method [ 67 ] . The AUC analysis rests on the binormal ROC model [ 36 ] and Fisher’s linear discriminant [ 30 ] and on exact null properties of the Mann–Whitney statistic [ 46 , 9 , 22 ] . Covariance estimation in the d ≳ n d\gtrsim n regime uses shrinkage [ 40 , 18 ] ; intrinsic dimension estimation uses maximum likelihood [ 41 , 45 ] with the two-NN estimator [ 28 ] as a cross-check.
